h1: The 8 Best Docking Stations for MacBook Air of 2026, Ranked & Reviewed
metaTitle: MacBook Air Docking Stations: Ranked & Reviewed
metaDescription: Ranked and reviewed by Primea: 8 docking stations for MacBook Air, from a certified Plugable Thunderbolt 4 dock to DisplayLink hubs, scored on displays.
summary: The Plugable TBT-UDM is the best overall, a certified Thunderbolt 4 dock with 100W charging and no drivers. The TobenONE 18-in-2 is the dual 4K choice through DisplayLink, the Anker DL6350 adds a third screen, and the WAVLINK reaches 5K. The cheaper PULWTOP, Anker 8-in-1 and UGREEN hubs cover budget and travel use.
intro: The MacBook Air has one hard limit that decides which dock you should buy. On most chips it drives a single external display natively. Any dock that advertises two monitors on an Air either leans on DisplayLink software to fake the second screen or quietly mirrors it, and a listing will not always tell you which. Buying on port count alone misses that entirely.

Our editors reviewed eight docks and hubs across that divide: one certified Thunderbolt dock for a clean single or 6K display, several DisplayLink docks for two or three screens, and plain hubs for travel. Rankings weigh display method, charging wattage, chip compatibility and port speeds, so check your Air's chip generation against each listing before ordering.

products.name: Plugable Thunderbolt 4 Dock for M4/M5 MacBook Air & Pro (TBT-UDM)
products.verdict: Certified Thunderbolt 4, 100W charging and a driverless setup.
products.description:
The TBT-UDM is the only certified Thunderbolt 4 dock here, running at 40Gbps with 100W charging. It drives dual 4K HDMI or one 6K display depending on your chip, adds six USB ports, an SD slot and Ethernet, and needs no drivers. That driverless link matters because it carries video natively, with no compression layer.

It ranks first because a certified controller keeps the connection stable, and it is the dock built for the newer Thunderbolt Airs. The DisplayLink hubs below reach more screens, but only by software and a driver install.

Buy it for a newer Air with one high-quality monitor. The caveat: the second display depends on your chip, and it needs a Thunderbolt port, so an older Air without one cannot use it. It also costs the most in the guide.
cons: Dual display depends on the chip
products.idealFor: Newer Airs with one high-quality monitor.
products.skipIf: Your Air has no Thunderbolt port.

products.name: TobenONE 18-in-2 Docking Station Dual Monitor for MacBook Pro/Air
products.verdict: DisplayLink dual 4K at 60Hz with a 150W power adapter and 2.5G Ethernet.
products.description:
The TobenONE 18-in-2 solves the Air's actual problem, a second monitor. DisplayLink pushes a second 4K signal at 60Hz through HDMI and USB-C, a 150W power adapter comes in the box, and the dock adds seven USB ports, 10Gbps USB-C, 2.5G Ethernet and an SD 4.0 reader.

It ranks second behind the Plugable because DisplayLink compresses video through a driver. For spreadsheets and calls, that is invisible. The 17-in-2 sibling is close but older, and the PULWTOP gives dual 4K for less with fewer ports.

Buy it if you need two extended screens on an Air. The caveats are a one-time driver install, compression on fast video and a large adapter brick. A dock that powers everything from a 150W supply needs desk space.
products.idealFor: Air owners who need two external screens.

products.name: Anker Docking Station DL6350, 10-Port Triple Display with DisplayLink
products.verdict: Three displays through DisplayLink with dual HDMI and DisplayPort.
products.description:
The DL6350 is the three-screen answer. It uses DisplayLink to feed dual HDMI plus DisplayPort across 10 ports, and works with Windows PCs as well as MacBook Air and Pro. Anker's driver support is mature, which counts when macOS updates break lesser drivers.

It ranks third because three screens is a niche need. The TobenONE gives two screens with more power and ports. If you do want three monitors on a fanless Air, nothing else here delivers that.

Buy it for a trading or monitoring desk where a wide wall of screens matters more than motion quality. The caveat: all three screens go through compression, and the driver is mandatory. Pay for this only if you will use the third screen, because it costs more than the dual-monitor docks.
cons: Higher price for a niche need
products.idealFor: Three-monitor desks on a MacBook Air.

products.name: WAVLINK USB C Docking Station Dual Monitor, Dual 5K/4K@60Hz
products.verdict: Dual displays up to 5K, with HDMI and DisplayPort and 130W charging.
products.description:
The WAVLINK 13-in-1 supports two displays up to 5K through DisplayLink, with two HDMI and two DisplayPort outputs, 130W Power Delivery, five USB ports and audio. It lists support for M1 to M4 Macs as well as Windows.

It ranks fourth because a 5K ceiling matters to few owners, and the TobenONE offers 2.5G Ethernet and a bundled adapter. What it does give you is mixed outputs, so a monitor with HDMI and another with DisplayPort connect without adapters.

Buy it if you own a high-resolution display or a mismatched pair of screens. Skip it if you want a driverless setup. With only five USB ports and no listed 2.5G Ethernet, it is thinner on connectivity than the TobenONE for similar money.

products.name: TobenONE 17-IN-2 MacBook Docking Station Dual 4K Monitor
products.verdict: Dual 4K, a 150W charger and compatibility from M1 through M5.
products.description:
The TobenONE 17-in-2 offers dual 4K through DisplayLink, a 150W charger, seven USB ports up to 10Gbps and 2.5G Ethernet. The listing states compatibility with M1 through M5 chips, which helps when an older Air and a newer one share a desk.

It ranks fifth because the 18-in-2 sits above it in the same line with a USB-C display output, and the specs are otherwise close. Next to the PULWTOP it adds a bigger charger and faster Ethernet, so it is the better buy if you want power and networking in one box.

Buy it when you want a bundled charger and the widest chip coverage. The caveats are DisplayLink compression and a large brick. Skip it if you want a native Thunderbolt link, which only the Plugable provides.
products.idealFor: Older and newer Airs sharing one desk.
products.skipIf: You want a native Thunderbolt link.

products.name: PULWTOP MacBook Pro Docking Station Dual Monitor 4K@60Hz
products.verdict: Dual HDMI at 4K and 60Hz for under $100.
products.description:
The PULWTOP is the cheapest way to get two screens on an Air. Dual HDMI at 4K and 60Hz runs through DisplayLink, with 10Gbps USB-A and USB-C data, SD and TF slots, a USB 2.0 port, Ethernet and PD charging passthrough. It sits in the $50 to $100 bucket.

It ranks sixth because the TobenONE models add chargers and faster Ethernet, and the brand is less known. The savings come with a driver install and no listed charger, so you must supply your own.

Buy it for a budget dual monitor desk where spreadsheets and email dominate. Skip it if brand support matters to you. A lesser known brand may be slower to update drivers when macOS changes, so keep the box and receipt.
products.skipIf: Brand support is important to you.

products.name: Anker Laptop Docking Station Dual Monitor, 8-in-1 USB C Hub
products.verdict: Dual HDMI, 85W Power Delivery and Gigabit Ethernet for little money.
products.description:
The Anker 8-in-1 is a plain USB-C hub with dual HDMI, 85W Power Delivery, Gigabit Ethernet and an SD reader, and it sits in the $50 to $100 bucket. The charger is not included.

It ranks seventh because on a base-chip Air a hub without DisplayLink will mirror the second screen instead of extending it, which defeats the purpose of two monitors. It beats the UGREEN on port count.

Buy it for a simple desk with one monitor, Ethernet and a card reader. The caveat is the dual HDMI claim: confirm that your Air supports two extended displays before expecting both to behave as separate desktops. Without a charger in the box, factor in a separate power brick of your own.
products.idealFor: One monitor, Ethernet and a card reader.
products.skipIf: You need two extended screens on a base chip.

products.name: UGREEN 10-in-1 USB C Docking Station, Revodok Pro 210
products.verdict: The smallest and cheapest pick here, with dual HDMI or one 8K output.
products.description:
The Revodok Pro 210 is a compact 10-in-1 hub with dual HDMI at 4K and 60Hz or one 8K at 30Hz, 100W Power Delivery, 5Gbps data, Gigabit Ethernet and SD and TF readers. It is the smallest and cheapest pick in the guide.

It ranks last because it is a hub, not a dock, and 5Gbps is the slowest data speed here. Dual display output also depends on your chip, so an Air may drive only one screen from it.

Buy it for travel and one extra monitor. The caveat: copying photos or video to an external SSD will be slower than on the 10Gbps docks. For a permanent desk, one of the TobenONE docks or the Plugable is a better foundation.
cons: Dual screens depend on your chip

whatMatters.detail: Most MacBook Air chips drive one external display natively. A hub that advertises dual HDMI will usually mirror the second screen on those, or extend it only with DisplayLink software. Check your Air's tech specs page for the supported external displays, then match the dock to that number before you shop.

DisplayLink adds extra screens by compressing video through a driver, and it needs a one-time install. It works well for documents and calls but can stutter on fast video. If you only need one screen, skip it and take a native dock. Look for the word DisplayLink in the listing, and check macOS support before you buy.

A MacBook Air needs far less than a Pro, roughly 30 to 45W. Any dock giving 65W or more charges it with room to spare. Look for passthrough wattage in the specs, and for a bundled charger if you want to avoid carrying a second brick. A dock without a charger needs your own, so add that cost.

Some docks list support for specific chips, such as M1 through M4 or M5. Check that your chip appears on the list, and that macOS is current, since driver support follows the operating system. Newer Airs may use Thunderbolt, while older ones use USB-C. Look in the listing compatibility section, not only the title, because titles often oversell compatibility.

5Gbps is fine for a keyboard and mouse. If you copy photos or video to an SSD, look for 10Gbps ports or Thunderbolt, which feel noticeably faster on large files. Compare the stated speed of each port, since a dock may mix speeds, and read whether the USB-C port is data only or also display capable.

faq.q: Can a MacBook Air run two external monitors?
faq.a: Natively, most cannot. With DisplayLink docks such as the TobenONE 18-in-2 or Anker DL6350 you can, at the cost of a driver install and compressed video that suits documents better than motion.

faq.q: Do I need a Thunderbolt dock for a MacBook Air?
faq.a: Not unless you want a native single-screen dock. The Plugable TBT-UDM is the Thunderbolt option and drives dual 4K or one 6K, depending on chip. Cheaper hubs cover the basics for a single screen and a few peripherals.

faq.q: Is the TobenONE worth more than the PULWTOP?
faq.a: If you want a charger included and faster Ethernet, yes. The TobenONE models bundle a 150W adapter and 2.5G Ethernet. For just two screens the PULWTOP is enough and costs far less, so the extras are the only real reason to upgrade.

faq.q: Will a hub charge my Air while docked?
faq.a: Yes, through passthrough Power Delivery. An Air needs about 30 to 45W, which every dock here exceeds, including the 85W Anker and the 100W UGREEN, though some require your own charger. Only the TobenONE docks bundle one.

faq.q: Does DisplayLink work well for video?
faq.a: It handles documents and calls fine but can struggle with fast motion, since the video is compressed. Prefer native output, like the Plugable, for gaming or video editing, where compression artifacts and latency show up.

faq.q: Can I use these docks with a Windows PC?
faq.a: The Anker DL6350 and WAVLINK both list Windows support, so a work PC and a MacBook can share one dock. Check each listing before assuming, since not all do, and Windows drivers may differ from the Mac ones.

finalTake: Buy the Plugable if one clean display is enough and your Air has Thunderbolt. Pick the TobenONE 18-in-2 for two screens, the Anker DL6350 for three, and the PULWTOP for the cheapest second monitor. Treat the Anker 8-in-1 and UGREEN as hubs that may only mirror a second display on a base chip.
